intro: The Daodejing and the Zhuangzi are the two great early books of Daoist thought. They speak of the Dao, the Way, and of acting without forcing. They teach with pictures: water, an empty bowl, an uncarved block, a swimmer, a cook and a frog.

In this unit you will learn the big ideas: Dao, wu wei, yin and yang, and de. Then you will read the images the books use to teach them. You will also learn that Daoism is studied as a philosophy and practiced by many people as a religion.
By the end, you can explain each big idea with a passage. You can tell what an image means to its readers. You can compare how Daoist books teach with how the Analects teaches.
bigQuestion: What do the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi teach about the Way, and why do they teach with pictures?

timeline.t: The Daodejing takes shape, many scholars think
Parts of the Daodejing are buried on bamboo at Guodian
Silk copies of the Daodejing are buried at Mawangdui
The Way of the Celestial Masters begins, tradition says
Early forms of the taijitu diagram appear in the Song dynasty
Legge publishes the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi in English

words.d: the Way; in the Daodejing, the nameless source and pattern of all things
'so of itself'; being natural or spontaneous, happening by its own nature
acting without forcing; effortless action that goes with the way things are
paired opposites, like shade and sun, that need each other and change into each other
the diagram of yin and yang, often drawn as a swirling circle
power or virtue; in the Daodejing, the quiet strength of following the Dao
the uncarved block; plain, whole simplicity in the Daodejing
a picture in words that helps explain an idea
open, empty space; in the Daodejing, what makes things useful
the way something looks from where you stand
an early organized Daoist movement, traditionally dated to about 142 CE

test.q: What does Daodejing 25 say about the Dao's name?
choices: The speaker does not know it and calls it Dao
It is written in the Analects
test.why: Chapter 25 says the true name is unknown.

test.q: Which chapter says the Dao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone?
In Zhuangzi 19, how does the swimmer survive the waterfall?
test.why: He goes with the water, not against it.

choices: The sunny side of a hill
test.why: Yang first meant the sunny side; yin the shady side.

test.q: In Daodejing 51, what does de do?
test.why: The Dao gives life, and de nourishes.

choices: It is studied as philosophy and practiced as a religion
test.why: Daoism is both a philosophy and a living religion.

test.q: What does Daodejing 8 say about water?
choices: It benefits all things and does not compete
test.why: Chapter 8 praises water for helping without competing.

test.q: In Daodejing 11, what makes a bowl useful?
What does the uncarved block stand for?
test.why: Pu is a picture of plain, whole simplicity.

test.q: What can villagers hear in Daodejing 80?
choices: The next village's roosters and dogs
test.why: They hear the next village but never visit.

test.q: How long has Cook Ding kept his knife sharp?
What does the frog in the well story teach about?
test.why: From the well, the frog thinks the sky is small.

test.q: Which Daodejing chapter ranks the barely-noticed leader best?
How do the Daodejing and Zhuangzi often teach, compared with the Analects?
test.why: They teach more through pictures and stories.

write.prompt: Choose one Daoist idea: wu wei or simplicity. Explain it using two or three passages, such as Daodejing 8, 11 or 37 and Zhuangzi 3 or 19 (Legge's translations, 1891). Tell what each passage says and how readers have understood it.
tips: Name the book and chapter each time.
Say 'the Daodejing says' or 'Daoists teach'; do not state your own belief as fact.
Explain the image before you explain the idea.
Use unit words like wu wei, pu and ziran.
